questions.stem: A 74-year-old man presented with fever and malaise. His past medical history included severe aortic stenosis and ascending aortic aneurysm, for which he received concomitant aortic valve replacement and aortic root repair 2 years previously. The patient had well-controlled diabetes but no other comorbidities. Physical exam revealed a new murmur. Investigations: Hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL HIV Ag/Ab negative Routine blood cultures ×3 pairs negative Mycobacterial blood culture positive after 2 weeks of incubation
questions.lead_in: What organism is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium chimaera This is a case of M. chimaera-related endocarditis following a valve replacement surgery. High level of suspicion is needed to make the diagnosis and to send the appropriate cultures. Incubation period for symptom presentation can be as long as 5 years. Slow rate of growth and absence of underlying immunodeficiency can help you eliminate the other options.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q35

parts.text: 2 agents that are approved for MRSA bacteremia.
An echo was performed, and the patient has a vegetation on a prosthetic valve. What agent to add?

cohort_answer.text: Vancomycin; Daptomycin. || Rifampin (x6 weeks) + gent (x2 weeks).

parts.text: What are the 5 most common GNR causing endocarditis? Name to genus level.
A patient has MRSA prosthetic valve endocarditis. Name the agents recommended for treatment according to IDSA guidelines and duration for each (dose, route, duration).

questions.model_answer:
a) Five most common gram-negative bacilli causing endocarditis (HACEK group, to genus level): Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella.
b) MRSA prosthetic valve endocarditis (IDSA/AHA guideline regimen): vancomycin IV for at least 6 weeks, PLUS rifampin orally/IV for at least 6 weeks, PLUS gentamicin IV for the first 2 weeks only (added for synergy, not the full duration).
questions.beyond_mandell: AHA/IDSA 2015 infective endocarditis guideline regimen for staphylococcal PVE.

questions.question: 21. 60 year old man has been having fever, weight loss and night sweats for 2 months. Physical examination is normal. There have been no recent exposures of any kind. No travel history. Past medical history is notable for coronary artery bypass grafting and aortic valve replacement with mechanical valve 18 months ago. TTE/TEE are normal.

parts.text: What infection needs to be considered in this patient?
What two diagnostic tests are recommended and would be helpful?
What is the treatment?

cohort_answer.text: NTM: M. chimaera. Diagnostic tests: Mycobacterial blood cultures; tissue samples for culture, sequencing or PCR. Treatment: prolonged course of Azithromycin, Ethambutol, and Rifampin (same as cavitary MAC); severe disease may require aminoglycosides; surgery often suggested if possible

parts.text: What is a treatment for MRSA prosthetic valve endocarditis according to IDSA guidelines (drug, route, dose, duration)?

cohort_answer.text: Vancomycin IV (~30 mg/kg/d in 2 doses, target trough 10-20), minimum six weeks. Rifampin IV/PO 900 mg in 3 divided doses, minimum 6 weeks. Gentamicin IV/IM 3 mg/kg/d in 2-3 divided doses, 2 weeks. Gentamicin should be administered for the initial 2 weeks of therapy with either beta-lactam or vancomycin-containing regimens; if a strain is resistant to gentamicin, a fluoroquinolone may be used if the strain is susceptible.

questions.question: A patient with a prosthetic valve has fever, murmur and several sets of blood cultures positive for E. faecium resistant to ampicillin, aminoglycosides, and vancomycin.

parts.text: Name two regimens that could be used for treatment.

questions.model_answer: Two regimens for VRE (E. faecium resistant to ampicillin, aminoglycosides, vancomycin) prosthetic valve endocarditis: (1) Daptomycin high-dose (10-12 mg/kg) plus a β-lactam (e.g. ampicillin, ceftaroline, or ertapenem) for synergy. (2) Linezolid (± another active agent such as an aminoglycoside if susceptible, or quinupristin-dalfopristin-based regimen as alternative).

questions.question: 70yo M with recent bioprosthetic aortic valve insertion with E faecalis in 4/4 blood cultures over 48 hours. Susceptible to ampicillin but high level resistance to both gentamicin and streptomycin.

parts.text: What is a diagnostic test you need to do and how would it change management?
Two micro bench characteristics of E faecalis
What is most common reason for aminoglycoside resistance and how is it acquired
What is your antibiotic regimen including duration

questions.model_answer:
a) Diagnostic test: confirm high-level aminoglycoside resistance (HLAR) testing to both gentamicin and streptomycin (already done here) - this determines that aminoglycoside synergy is not achievable, changing management to a dual beta-lactam regimen (ampicillin plus ceftriaxone) instead of ampicillin plus an aminoglycoside.
b) Two bench characteristics of E. faecalis: (1) catalase-negative, gram-positive cocci in chains/pairs (2) growth in bile-esculin agar and in 6.5% NaCl broth (PYR test positive).
c) Most common cause of aminoglycoside resistance in enterococci: production of an aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme (most commonly the bifunctional AAC(6')-APH(2'') enzyme), acquired via plasmid-mediated horizontal gene transfer.
d) Antibiotic regimen: ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (dual beta-lactam synergistic therapy) for a total of 6 weeks, given HLAR precludes aminoglycoside synergy.

questions.question: A patient has E. faecium prosthetic valve endocarditis resistant to penicillin, vancomycin and gentamicin.

parts.text: What are 2 regimens that you could use to treat?

cohort_answer.text: Linezolid, IV/PO, 600 mg q12h, >(?) 6 weeks. Daptomycin 10-12 mg/kg/dose, >(?) 6 weeks.

questions.question: Man 3 weeks out from bioprosthetic AV, presents with systemic symptoms and BC growing E. faecalis susceptible to ampicillin, resistant to high level gentamicin and streptomycin.

parts.text: Name 1 investigation you would do and how it would affect your management of this patient.
What is the mechanism of aminoglycoside resistance in this patient?
What treatment will you prescribe for him?
List the result of 2 biochemical tests for this organism.

cohort_answer.text: Investigation: TEE or repeat blood cultures; if confirms IE, would change duration of treatment and likely need for surgery. Mechanism: Aminoglycoside modifying enzymes (acetyltransferases, phosphotransferases, or nucleotidyltransferases) altering the aminoglycoside and its ability to bind 30S ribosome subunit. Treatment: Ampicillin 2g IV q4h + Ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h x6 weeks. Biochemical tests: Catalase negative; Bile Esculin positive; PYR positive

questions.question: AM 18. MRSA prosthetic valve IE what drugs to treat and duration for each component. According to the IDSA/ATS guidelines (2)

parts.text: Prosthetic valve IE treatment
a. Other than congenital cardiac - which 3 conditions require prophylaxis for dental procedure (1.5)
b. If going for a colonoscopy in a cyanotic unrepaired, what if any prophylaxis do you recommend (1)

cohort_answer.text: Prosthetic valve IE: 6 weeks total therapy - Vancomycin + Rifampin x6 weeks, plus gentamicin for first 2 weeks. a) Previous infective endocarditis; transplant with valvulopathy; prosthetic valve (congenital cardiac ones: cyanotic heart disease within 6 months of repair, or repaired with ongoing non-epithelialized areas). b) No prophylaxis (respiratory tract biopsy IS an indication for prophylaxis; debridement of infected skin/soft tissue).

questions.question: AM 19. Lady with PVE growing E. faecium resistant to penicillin, HLAR, and vancomycin. What 2 treatment regimens (2)

parts.text: What 2 treatment regimens

questions.model_answer: Two treatment regimens for penicillin-resistant, HLAR, vancomycin-resistant (VRE) E. faecium PVE: (1) Linezolid (2) Daptomycin (typically high-dose, often combined with ampicillin or ceftaroline for synergy).
questions.beyond_mandell: Combination daptomycin + beta-lactam synergy for VRE endocarditis reflects more recent literature beyond this chapter excerpt.

questions.question: E faecalis bacteremia with a prosthetic valve 3 weeks ago. It has HLAR to gent and strepto.

parts.text: What test is required next which will impact treatment?
What treatment regimen and duration?
What's the most common enterococcus resistance to AG and how is it acquired?
Two bench biochemicals for identification

questions.model_answer: a) Next test: repeat/confirm high-level aminoglycoside resistance testing to both gentamicin AND streptomycin specifically (since HLAR to one does not preclude synergy with the other) - this determines whether an aminoglycoside can still be used synergistically. b) Treatment regimen/duration: ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (dual β-lactam synergy, avoids aminoglycoside toxicity) for 6 weeks (prosthetic valve endocarditis); if not HLAR to streptomycin, ampicillin plus streptomycin is an alternative. c) Most common enterococcal aminoglycoside resistance: bifunctional enzyme AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2'')-Ia (aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme) conferring high-level resistance to gentamicin (and most aminoglycosides except streptomycin); acquired via plasmid-mediated horizontal gene transfer/conjugation. d) Two bench biochemical tests for identification: (1) Pyrrolidonyl arylamidase (PYR) test - positive in Enterococcus. (2) Growth in 6.5% NaCl broth and bile-esculin hydrolysis (positive for Enterococcus, distinguishes from Streptococcus).

questions.question: Recent cardiac surgery for valve replacement, now with E. fecalis bacteremia.

parts.text: Name 2 rapid test for identification in lab
Shows high level resistance to AMG; mechanism
Therapy and duration

questions.model_answer: a) Two rapid identification tests: (1) Pyrrolidonyl arylamidase (PYR) test - rapid, positive in Enterococcus. (2) Bile-esculin hydrolysis plus growth in 6.5% NaCl - both positive in Enterococcus, distinguishing from streptococci. b) High-level aminoglycoside resistance mechanism: bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2'')-Ia, plasmid-mediated (horizontally transferable), confers resistance to gentamicin (and most aminoglycosides, sparing streptomycin which has a different mechanism). c) Therapy and duration: ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (dual β-lactam synergy) for 6 weeks given prosthetic valve endocarditis.

parts.text: A) What is the reason for testing AG high level resistance?
B) What is the mechanism of high level resistance?
C) If streptomycin was used instead of gentamicin, what is the major disadvantage?

cohort_answer.text:
If high level AG resistance exists, we cannot use AG (except streptomycin) for synergistic treatment
Bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6')-IE-APH(2")-Ia
Need access to lab for rapid streptomycin level testing; Need CrCl >50; Lack of familiarity amongst clinicians for streptomycin use; Drug availability; High rate of ototoxicity which may not be reversible

questions.question: A man is 3 weeks post aortic valve replacement with bioprosthesis, presenting with fevers and chills. Four sets of blood cultures are positive for Enterococcus faecalis. The isolate is susceptible to ampicillin, but demonstrates high-level resistance to gentamicin and streptomycin.

parts.text: What other test is needed for this patient (be specific)?
Name two rapid microbiologic tests that can be used to identify enterococcus species?
Why test for high-level resistance to Gentamicin?
What is the mechanism of high-level aminoglycoside resistance?
With what agent(s) will you treat this patient and for how long?

cohort_answer.text:
TEE
PYR +; faecalis and faecium are non-motile, casseliflavus and gallinarum are motile and casseliflavus has yellow pigment; MALDI-TOF; interacts with Lancefield group D antisera
Bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6')-IE-APH(2")-Ia
Ampicillin 2g IV q4h + CRO 2g IV q12h for 6 weeks

questions.question: 70M have AVR 3 weeks ago, now fevers/chills. Blood cultures 4/4 Enterococcus faecalis. Susceptible to ampicillin but high-level resistance to gentamicin

parts.text: What is one investigation that you would want to do, and why?
What are two microbiologic tests that would help in rapidly identifying Enterococcus?
What is the most common mechanism of aminoglycoside resistance, and how is it transmitted between bacteria?
What is your recommended management? (2 points)

questions.model_answer: a) Investigation: transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) - higher sensitivity than TTE for detecting prosthetic valve vegetations/abscess in suspected prosthetic valve endocarditis. b) Two rapid microbiologic identification tests: (1) Pyrrolidonyl arylamidase (PYR) test. (2) Bile-esculin hydrolysis with growth in 6.5% NaCl broth. c) Most common aminoglycoside resistance mechanism: bifunctional enzyme AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2'')-Ia (aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme), transmitted via plasmid-mediated horizontal gene transfer (conjugation) between bacteria. d) Recommended management (2 points): (1) Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (dual β-lactam synergistic therapy, avoiding aminoglycoside given HLR to gentamicin) - note streptomycin susceptibility should still be checked as an alternative synergy option. (2) Total duration of 6 weeks IV therapy for prosthetic valve endocarditis; surgical consultation given prosthetic valve involvement.

questions.question: Prosthetic valve enterococcal IE. Patient with prosthetic valve growing persistent enterococcus in blood, was also positive 4 weeks ago. Isolate is S to ampicillin but high level resistance to Genta + Streptomycin. TTE is negative for vegetations.

parts.text: A) What is your dx?
B) The service has started high dose ampicillin, do you agree? Justify your answer
C) What aspect of this case would be considered indications for surgery?

cohort_answer.text:
Possible prosthetic valve IE
Agree but suggest adding Ceftriaxone 2g iV q12h for synergy. Min duration for prosthetic valve IE is 6 weeks
No surgical indications at this time (unless it was relapsing PVE). "Standard indications for surgery are severe heart failure, severe valve dysfunction, prosthetic valve infection, invasion beyond the valve leaflets, recurrent systemic embolization, large mobile vegetations, or persistent sepsis despite adequate antibiotic therapy for more than 5-7 days"
